questions.question: Angular or React — which should I pick for a new project, and why?
questions.title: Angular vs React: Choosing a Frontend Framework
questions.direct_answer: Angular is a full, opinionated framework (compiler, DI, routing, forms built in); React is a library (just components — you add routing/forms yourself). Pick Angular for large, structured teams that want conventions and batteries-included; pick React for flexibility and a large ecosystem where you assemble your own stack. Neither is universally 'better' — the choice is about fit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate the framework-vs-library trade-off (convention vs flexibility) and name when each fits, rather than picking a favorite.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking based on popularity alone, or claiming one is 'better' without naming the trade-off (opinionated batteries vs flexible library).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame it as framework-vs-library: Angular = opinionated platform (routing, forms, DI included); React = flexible library (you compose). Match to team and project.

sections.title: What Angular and React Each Are
sections.content: Angular (by Google) is a full, opinionated framework: it ships a compiler, dependency injection, routing, forms, and HTTP out of the box. React (by Meta) is a library: it gives you components and the virtual DOM, and you add routing, forms, and state management yourself (or via the ecosystem). The choice isn't 'which is better' — it's 'which fits your team and project.' Angular suits large, structured teams that want one convention for everything; React suits teams that want to pick each piece and value a huge ecosystem.

sections.title: The Framework-vs-Library Decision
sections.content:
The decision is about how much the framework decides for you.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[New project] --> B{Team & project?}
  B -->|Large team, want one convention| C[Angular: batteries-included]
  B -->|Want to pick each piece| D[React: flexible library]
  C --> E[Routing, forms, DI all built in]
  D --> F[Add React Router, a form lib, state mgmt]
```

sections.title: Creating a component in each — the difference in ceremony
Angular vs React at a Glance
Common Mistakes When Choosing
items: Picking on popularity alone, ignoring team fit and project size.
Assuming React is 'less' because it's a library — you still wire routing/forms/state.
Forgetting Angular's build/CLI overhead for a small app where React (or a simpler tool) fits.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Angular is a full framework (routing, forms, DI included); React is a library (you add those).
The choice is convention (Angular) vs flexibility (React) — neither is universally better.
Angular suits large, structured teams wanting one convention; React suits teams wanting to pick each piece.
React's ecosystem is larger; Angular's is more unified and batteries-included.
Match the tool to the team and project, not to popularity.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Angular and React are the two main frontend choices, and the difference is framework versus library. Angular is a full, opinionated framework by Google — it ships routing, forms, dependency injection, and HTTP out of the box, so a large team gets one convention for everything. React by Meta is a library — it gives you components and the virtual DOM, and you add routing, forms, and state management yourself or from the ecosystem, so you compose your own stack and have a larger, more flexible ecosystem. Neither is universally better. Angular suits large, structured teams that want batteries-included conventions; React suits teams that want to pick each piece and value flexibility. The mistake is choosing on popularity alone — the right frame is which fits your team and project.
